The else suite runs only when the try block finishes normally without any exception being raised. If an exception is raised part‑way through the try, execution jumps to the matching except clause and then continues after the whole try/except/else/finally construct. If two except clauses could both match, the one that appears first in the source code is the one that runs.

If we only needed the top‑k scores, a heap would be another option, but for the full leaderboard a balanced BST is the most appropriate choice.

turns.prompt: You insert the keys 1, 2, 3, …, n in that order into a plain (not self-balancing) binary search tree. What shape does the tree take, and what do search and insert cost? How do self-balancing trees such as AVL or red-black trees avoid this, and what do their operations cost?
turns.answer: Inserting 1, 2, 3,…, n into an ordinary BST always puts each new key to the right of the previous one, so the tree collapses into a right‑leaning chain of height n (Θ(n)). Consequently a search or an insert must walk down that chain, giving Θ(n) time per operation and Θ(n²) total to build the tree. Self‑balancing trees such as AVL or red‑black trees perform rotations (and recolorings for red‑black) after each insertion or deletion to keep the height bounded by O(log n). Because the height stays logarithmic, search, insert and delete all run in Θ(log n) worst‑case time.

grade.rationale: The candidate correctly identified that inserting sorted keys into a plain BST creates a degenerate chain of height O(n) with O(n) operations, and explained that self-balancing trees use rotations to maintain O(log n) height and operation costs.
